name: H. J. R. Murray
knownFor: The historian whose books are the standard histories of chess and of board games.
bio: Harold James Ruthven Murray was the eldest son of Sir James Murray, the first editor of the Oxford English Dictionary, and as a schoolboy he helped his father by producing over 27,000 quotations for it. He read mathematics at Balliol College, Oxford, and worked as a schoolmaster, a headmaster and then a school inspector.

He learned chess as an adult and, encouraged in 1897 to research its history, spent thirteen years teaching himself Arabic and German and reading the world's great chess libraries. The result, A History of Chess (1913), proposed an Indian origin for the game and remains the most widely accepted account.

works.title: A History of Board-Games Other than Chess
A Short History of Chess
works.note: a shorter, more popular book, published after his death

events.text: Graduated from Balliol College, Oxford, with a first in mathematics.
Became headmaster of Ormskirk Grammar School in Lancashire.
Began thirteen years of research into the history of chess.
Appointed a school inspector; in 1928 he joined the Board of Education.
Published A History of Board-Games Other than Chess.
Died; most of his unpublished papers are in the Bodleian Library.

relevance: Murray's 1952 book is the first large English-language survey of the world's board games other than chess, from Mancala-type games to draughts. It remains a landmark, although parts of it have been criticised — his scepticism about the great age of Go, for example, has not held up.
influence: His History of Chess is recognised as the standard reference on the subject, and the Indian-origin theory he proposed is still the most widely accepted.

dateDiscrepancy: The Library of Congress authority record gives the birth year as 1869; Wikipedia and Wikidata give 24 June 1868, as does The Oxford Companion to Chess (Hooper & Whyld, 2nd ed., pp. 265–66), which Wikipedia cites. 1868 is used here.
